seed: Shannon Byrne Susko, System by System post Build Up Your 3-5 Differentiators and worksheet; training of 27-Sep-2026; Byron Darlison, How I Create Strategy; Activity Fit Map playbook, Byron’s rulings of 27-Sep, 30-Sep and 9-Oct-2026 (name, keep 3 to 5, then draw dependencies from the most connected; a group with no lines; descriptor; sleep on it), order confirmed by Byron, 25-Nov-2026.

slides.title: What must we do to make the whole 3HAG line true?
slides.support: Each leader writes 5 to 7 activities alone, one on each sticky note.
body: The whole line: where you will lead, what you will maintain and what you will let drop.
An activity can be something to stop doing.
Present your activities. Put them all on the board.
notes: The objective is to build the company’s 3 to 5 differentiators from the ground up. Do not start from the attributes at the top of the line and work down. That gives generic answers.
Keep asking the one question: what activities need to be in place to make the whole 3HAG line true?
Each leader presents their activities. Start grouping similar ones as they go up.
slides.headline: What must we do to make the whole 3HAG line true?

slides.title: Group the activities. Name each group.
slides.support: Most teams end up with 4 to 6 groups.
body: Name each group for exactly what it will accomplish.
“Support” is too generic. Ask again: what will this group accomplish?
Test: tell your strategy using only the group names. If you cannot, rename.
notes: Name each group together. The name says what will be true when that group of activities is in place.
Ask why the group matters. Expect to ask about five times before the name tells the team’s own story.
Then test the whole set. If the team cannot tell the company’s strategy using only the names, the names are too generic. Rename.
Do not skip this step. Take the time it needs.
slides.headline: Group the activities. Name each group.

slides.title: Agree your 3 to 5 differentiators.
slides.support: Keep the strongest groups. Each one heads a swim lane.
body: Check back against your 3HAG line: every place you will lead has a group behind it.
Each one serves a need of your Core Customer.
A group you do not keep can stay as a supporting activity.
Give each a short descriptor: what is true when it is achieved.
notes: Most teams end up with 4 to 6 groups. Agree the 3 to 5 that carry the strategy before anyone draws an arrow.
Check each group back against the Attribution Framework. Which chosen attribute does it move? Which Core Customer need does it serve?
A group that connects to nothing the market values is a task, not a differentiator.
The descriptor heads the swim lane. It keeps the team aligned after people forget the workshop.
slides.headline: Agree your 3 to 5 differentiators.

slides.title: Example: an Activity Fit Map.
slides.support: Four differentiators and their activities. Each arrow shows what one depends on.

artwork.alt: An example Activity Fit Map. Four differentiators each hold three activities. A Named Person for 90 Days depends on Live in a Day. Live in a Day and One Flat Price both depend on Standard, Not Custom.

notes: The same subscription company as the earlier examples. Its 3HAG line leads on speed of setup, price predictability and support from a person. Reporting and customization drop.
The example company kept four differentiators. Then it drew the arrows.
Live in a Day and One Flat Price each depend on Standard, Not Custom. One product for everyone keeps setup fast and the price flat.
A Named Person for 90 Days depends on Live in a Day. When setup is fast, the contact has time for the customer.
In this example, Standard, Not Custom explains the lower reporting and customization scores.
This is an example. Do not recommend these differentiators to a team.
slides.headline: Example: an Activity Fit Map.

slides.title: What depends on what?
slides.support: Draw an arrow from each differentiator to the one it depends on. Start with the most connected.

artwork.alt: The four example differentiators by name, with arrows showing which depends on which.

body: A differentiator can depend on more than one other.
One with no arrows is either what sets you apart or a task. Ask which.
notes: Draw the arrows only between the 3 to 5 the team kept.
Take the most connected differentiator first. Ask of each other one: does this depend on that? Draw the arrow when the team agrees.
It is rare to get this far and find they are not connected. The connections are what make the strategy hard to copy.
Take a break here. The team comes back to the map with fresh eyes before it lays the differentiators over time.
Let the team sleep on the differentiators before they are final. Day 2 opens by asking what anyone would change.
slides.headline: What depends on what?
